blocks.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the fertility clinic because she has been unable to conceive after two years of regular, unprotected intercourse.
Tasks:
Take a focused history.
Explain the major causes of female factor infertility.
Outline appropriate examinations and investigations.
Discuss management options according to the likely cause.
A woman with irregular menstruation and hirsutism.
A woman with previous pelvic inflammatory disease.
A woman with severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia.
A woman with previous uterine evacuation and scanty menstruation.
A woman with reduced ovarian reserve who wishes to conceive.
Female factor infertility refers to infertility attributable wholly or partly to a condition affecting the female reproductive system.
The major categories are:
Failure to release an egg regularly, as may occur in PCOS, hypothalamic dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia or primary ovarian insufficiency.
Tubal obstruction or damage, pelvic adhesions and endometriosis that interfere with egg pickup, fertilisation or embryo transport.
Cavity-distorting fibroids, endometrial polyps, intrauterine adhesions and selected cervical abnormalities.
Reduced follicular reserve and declining oocyte quality, particularly with increasing age. Ovarian reserve is not identical to the ability to conceive naturally.
Other contributors include endometriosis, chronic medical conditions, medications, sexual factors and unexplained infertility after an appropriate evaluation.
Start by establishing rapport and acknowledging the emotional impact of infertility.
Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Ensure privacy and obtain consent.
Explain the purpose of the consultation.
Ask whether the patient would like her partner present.
Explain that both partners may need assessment.
Maintain a non-judgmental approach.

“Hello, my name is …, and I am one of the doctors in the gynaecology clinic. I understand that you have been trying to conceive without success. I appreciate that this can be a difficult experience. I would like to ask about your menstrual cycles, previous pregnancies, gynaecological history, medical conditions and your partner's reproductive health. This will help us identify possible causes and plan the appropriate investigations. Is that alright with you?”

content_groups.group_title: A. History of the presenting complaint

blocks.text: Ask:
How long have you been trying to conceive?
When did you stop using contraception?
How frequently do you have intercourse?
Have you ever been pregnant?
Have you had any miscarriages or ectopic pregnancies?
Have you undergone previous fertility investigations?
Has your menstrual cycle changed?
Have you previously been diagnosed with PCOS, endometriosis, fibroids or tubal disease?
Clarify whether this is primary or secondary infertility and assess the duration of attempts relative to the patient's age.
Ask about:
Age at menarche.
Last menstrual period.
Cycle length and regularity.
Duration and volume of bleeding.
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea.
Dysmenorrhoea.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Hot flushes or vaginal dryness.
Hirsutism, acne or scalp hair thinning.
Galactorrhoea.
Interpret the pattern rather than relying on a single symptom.

rows: Primary ovarian insufficiency or other hypo-oestrogenic states
Amenorrhoea with substantial weight loss or excessive exercise

blocks.text: Regular menstrual cycles make ovulation more likely, but they do not establish tubal patency or exclude every ovulatory disorder.
Ask about all previous pregnancies, their outcomes and any complications.
Specifically explore:
Miscarriages and their management.
Ectopic pregnancies.
Terminations of pregnancy.
Caesarean sections and other uterine surgery.
Postpartum infection or retained products of conception.
Uterine evacuation or hysteroscopy.
This may identify acquired tubal damage or intrauterine adhesions.
Ask about:
Pelvic inflammatory disease.
Previous sexually transmitted infections.
Endometriosis.
Fibroids and endometrial polyps.
Ovarian cysts or ovarian surgery.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Genital tuberculosis when epidemiologically relevant.
Cervical procedures and relevant screening history.
Clinical pearl: A history of PID or ectopic pregnancy raises suspicion of tubal disease even if the patient has regular menstrual cycles and no current pelvic pain.
Ask about diabetes, thyroid disease, renal or liver disease, autoimmune conditions, pituitary disease, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and medications that may affect reproductive function.
Also ask about symptoms of thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia and androgen excess.
Ask sensitively about intercourse frequency, dyspareunia, vaginal dryness, libido, penetration difficulties and the partner's erectile or ejaculatory function.
Do not assume that infertility is exclusively a female problem.
Explore:
Weight changes and nutritional status.
Smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs.
Exercise patterns.
Occupational exposures.
Family history of early menopause or infertility.
Emotional distress, relationship pressure and treatment expectations.
Offer support and avoid blaming the patient for her weight, lifestyle or reproductive history.
The examination should be guided by the history and symptoms. Obtain consent, provide appropriate exposure and offer a chaperone for an intimate examination according to local practice.
Assess:
Height, weight and BMI.
Blood pressure and other vital signs when indicated.
Hirsutism, acne and androgenic hair loss.
Thyroid enlargement or other signs of thyroid disease.
Galactorrhoea when clinically indicated and with consent.
Signs of hypo-oestrogenism.
Features of systemic illness.
Look for:
Previous surgical scars.
Abdominal masses.
Tenderness.
Organ enlargement.
Other relevant pelvic pathology.
Perform when indicated by the history or symptoms.
Assess:
External genital anatomy and signs of infection.
Vaginal discharge.
Cervical abnormalities.
Uterine size, shape and mobility.
Adnexal masses or tenderness.
Pelvic tenderness, nodularity or reduced organ mobility that may suggest endometriosis or adhesions.

rows: Ovarian cyst or other adnexal pathology
Does not exclude tubal disease or ovulatory dysfunction

subsections.subsection_title: How to report findings in the OSCE

blocks.text: “This is a 27-year-old woman presenting with primary infertility and irregular menstrual cycles. She also has hirsutism and acne, suggesting androgen excess and possible ovulatory dysfunction due to PCOS. I would investigate alternative endocrine causes, assess ovulatory function, arrange pelvic ultrasound where indicated, obtain semen analysis from her partner and assess tubal patency as appropriate.”

“This is a 31-year-old woman with two years of infertility and a history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Tubal damage is a significant possibility. I would arrange assessment of tubal patency, evaluate ovulatory function as indicated and obtain semen analysis from her partner.”

“This is a woman presenting with infertility, severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia. These features raise suspicion of endometriosis. I would arrange appropriate pelvic imaging, consider specialist assessment and discuss management in relation to her fertility goals.”

“This is a woman with infertility and markedly reduced menstrual flow following uterine evacuation. Intrauterine adhesions are a differential diagnosis. I would assess the uterine cavity using appropriate imaging and consider hysteroscopy if indicated.”
Investigations should identify the likely cause while avoiding unnecessary tests.
Menstrual history is the initial assessment.
Serum progesterone may be measured when confirmation of ovulation is needed, approximately seven days before the expected next menstruation.
In irregular cycles, investigate the underlying cause and individualise the timing of hormonal testing.

rows: Suspected thyroid dysfunction or testing according to local fertility guidance
Suspected ovarian insufficiency or assessment of amenorrhoea
Hirsutism, acne or other signs of androgen excess
Estimation of ovarian reserve and anticipated response to ovarian stimulation in appropriate settings
Relevant metabolic risk factors, including suspected PCOS

blocks.text: AMH should not be used alone to determine whether a woman can conceive naturally. Ovarian reserve tests are most useful when interpreted alongside age, history and the planned treatment.
Transvaginal ultrasound, when appropriate and acceptable, assesses:
Uterine anatomy.
Fibroids and endometrial polyps.
Endometrial appearance.
Ovarian morphology and antral follicle count.
Adnexal masses.
Features of endometriosis or other pelvic pathology.
A normal ultrasound does not exclude tubal obstruction or all forms of endometriosis.
Contrast is introduced through the cervix and radiographs assess the uterine cavity and fallopian tube patency.
An ultrasound-based technique that uses contrast to assess whether the fallopian tubes are patent.
Direct assessment of the pelvis and tubal dye passage. Reserved for selected cases, such as suspected endometriosis or other pelvic pathology.
Exclude pregnancy and assess for active genital tract infection before appropriate uterine or tubal procedures.
Hysteroscopy for suspected intrauterine adhesions or cavity pathology.
MRI for selected complex uterine or deep endometriosis assessments.
Genetic investigations when primary ovarian insufficiency or another specific inherited condition is suspected.
Additional endocrine investigations based on clinical findings.
Arrange semen analysis as part of the couple's evaluation, even if the history appears to suggest a female cause.
The following scenarios are common examination patterns.

items: Case 1: A 25-year-old woman with irregular cycles and hirsutism

blocks.text: Most likely consideration: PCOS with possible ovulatory dysfunction.
Investigations: Appropriate endocrine tests, assessment of metabolic risk and pelvic ultrasound when indicated. Evaluate the male partner and tubal patency as appropriate.

items: Case 2: A 30-year-old woman with previous PID

blocks.text: Most likely consideration: Tubal-factor infertility.
Investigations: Tubal patency testing, semen analysis and ovulatory assessment according to the history.
Case 3: A 32-year-old woman with severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia
Most likely consideration: Endometriosis.
Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound and specialist assessment. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.

items: Case 4: A 34-year-old woman with amenorrhoea and hot flushes

blocks.text: Most likely consideration: Primary ovarian insufficiency or another cause of hypo-oestrogenism.
Investigations: Appropriate hormonal assessment and further evaluation guided by the findings.
Case 5: A 29-year-old woman with scanty menstruation after dilatation and curettage
Most likely consideration: Intrauterine adhesions.
Investigations: Assessment of the uterine cavity, with hysteroscopy when indicated.
Management depends on the underlying cause, age, duration of infertility, ovarian reserve where relevant, tubal status, semen parameters and the couple's preferences.
Encourage regular intercourse every 2–3 days.
Review medications and optimise chronic medical conditions.
Encourage smoking cessation and avoidance of recreational drugs.
Promote a balanced diet and healthy weight.
Recommend folic acid, generally 400 micrograms daily for women at usual risk, with higher doses for specific indications.
Offer emotional support and realistic counselling.

rows: Address metabolic factors; letrozole is generally first-line ovulation induction for appropriate patients when no other infertility factor is identified
Treat the underlying disorder and optimise thyroid status before and during pregnancy as appropriate
Identify the cause and treat accordingly; dopamine agonists may be indicated in selected patients
Specialist counselling, assessment of underlying causes and discussion of reproductive options
Selected surgery or IVF depending on disease severity, age and other fertility factors
Individualised management; consider fertility goals when choosing medical treatment or surgery
Consider treatment when the lesion is likely to affect reproductive outcomes
Specialist assessment and possible hysteroscopic adhesiolysis
Expectant management in selected couples, ovarian stimulation with IUI or IVF according to clinical circumstances and local guidance

blocks.text: Important: Ovulation induction should not be started indiscriminately before considering pregnancy status and other infertility factors, particularly tubal disease and semen abnormalities.
Ovulation induction: Medication to stimulate ovulation in selected patients.
IUI: Prepared sperm is introduced into the uterus around ovulation in appropriate clinical circumstances.
IVF: Eggs are collected and fertilised in the laboratory, followed by embryo transfer.
ICSI: A single sperm is injected into an egg during IVF, generally for selected indications such as significant male-factor infertility.
Discuss benefits, limitations, financial costs, multiple pregnancy risks where relevant and the likelihood of success based on individual circumstances.
Refer to a fertility specialist when there is:
Female age 35 years or older with six months of unsuccessful attempts, or earlier when indicated.
Female age over 40 years, requiring prompt assessment.
Amenorrhoea or significant menstrual irregularity.
Suspected tubal disease or significant endometriosis.
Suspected primary ovarian insufficiency.
Severe male-factor infertility.
Prolonged infertility or unsuccessful initial treatment.
Q1. What are the major causes of female factor infertility?
Answer: Ovulatory disorders, tubal and pelvic disease, uterine or cervical abnormalities, age-related decline in fertility and selected ovarian disorders. Male factors may coexist.
Q2. What is the commonest ovulatory disorder associated with infertility?
Answer: PCOS is a common cause of anovulatory infertility. However, the underlying cause should be established rather than assuming that every woman with irregular cycles has PCOS.
Q3. How do you investigate suspected tubal-factor infertility?
Answer: HSG or HyCoSy can assess tubal patency. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation is reserved for selected cases where pelvic pathology is suspected or another surgical indication exists.
Q4. Does a normal pelvic ultrasound exclude endometriosis?
Answer: No. Superficial endometriosis may not be visible on ultrasound, although specialist imaging can identify some forms of deep endometriosis and endometriomas.
Q5. What is the role of AMH?
Answer: AMH helps estimate ovarian reserve and predict response to ovarian stimulation. It does not independently determine natural fertility or guarantee success with IVF.
Q6. What is the first-line treatment for PCOS-related anovulatory infertility?
Answer: Letrozole is generally first-line for appropriate patients with PCOS-related anovulatory infertility when other infertility factors have been excluded or appropriately addressed.
Q7. What is unexplained infertility?
Answer: Infertility in which an appropriate evaluation of ovulatory function, tubal patency and semen parameters has not identified a cause.
Q8. Why should both partners be investigated?
Answer: Infertility may be attributable to either partner or to combined factors. Parallel assessment avoids unnecessary delays and helps select appropriate treatment.
Assuming irregular cycles automatically mean PCOS.
Assuming regular cycles guarantee normal fertility.
Ordering AMH as a stand-alone fertility test.
Forgetting to assess tubal patency.
Failing to obtain a semen analysis from the male partner.
Performing invasive investigations without an indication.
Starting ovulation induction without considering other infertility factors.
Ignoring the emotional impact of infertility.
Promising that IVF or another treatment will guarantee pregnancy.
Use this to recall the major female reproductive factors:
O — Ovulation.
T — Tubal patency.
U — Uterine environment.
O — Ovarian reserve and age-related factors.
Remember that male-factor assessment must accompany this framework.
P — Period irregularity.
C — Clinical or biochemical androgen excess.
O — Ovarian morphology where relevant.
S — Screen for alternative causes and associated metabolic risk.
PCOS is diagnosed using accepted clinical criteria after excluding relevant alternative diagnoses; ultrasound is not mandatory in every case.
